lines.note: The header reads I ANTES DO B, with no clear final stop. Small isolated ink traces above and below the gap between D and O cannot confidently be identified as punctuation; retain DO rather than inventing an apostrophe or other sign.

runs.text: Porco do mato, mas não ſe vſa ſem compo-

lines.note: I means wild boar and is said to occur only in compounds. The headword is capital I, not OCR lowercase i; compo- continues into composição on the next row.
Inoco illustrates a young wild boar, literally a boar's offspring. Sição completes the preceding composition restriction; the Portuguese gloss is Filho de porco do mato.
Inoqi names a boar's teeth or tusks. Restore the visible paragraph sign introducing this additional compound example.

runs.text: Des das dez horas tè as doze.

lines.note: Ino cocu is the boar hour, glossed here as from ten to twelve. Retain this historical explanation without substituting a modern time scheme; the initial is I, and the visible paragraph sign is restored.

runs.text: Tea daranha, mas não ſe entendera ſe não,

lines.note: A separate I means a spider's web. The source says this word will not be understood except in the expression continued below; Tea daranha and the terminal comma are retained.
Cumono i is the spider-web expression, with Idem confirming the preceding meaning. The initial c is lowercase in the scan and is not capitalized editorially.
Another I means the stomach, but the usual expression is Ino fu. Retain printed Eſtamago and all three abbreviation tildes in cõmũmẽte; the isolated headword is capital I.
I, iru, ita gives the principal forms of the verb meaning to be or stay. The gloss is Estar; this is independent of the following homophonous shooting verb.
This I, iru, ita means to aim or shoot, distinct from the preceding verb of remaining. The gloss begins with shooting a firearm and continues after eſpin-.
Garda completes eſpingarda, with a bow as the other weapon. Yumi, teppôuo iru gives the Japanese example; the circumflex on teppô is visible and retained.
The example is translated as shooting with a bow or firearm. This row closes the shooting verb and has no Japanese material of its own.
Another I, iru, ita means to cast metal. Caneuo iru illustrates casting a bell, as shown by the Portuguese sino across the following line break; retain Fũ without an added hyphen.
Dirſino completes Fundir sino. The next example reads Nabeuo iru, casting a pot: restore the worn a rather than OCR Nibe, supported by surviving ink and the following panela gloss.
La completes panella, which may be of iron, copper, or similar material. This closes the casting verb before the I-before-B subheading.

zones.label: Column 1, part 2
zones.note: Enlarged initial I spans the first two body rows.

lines.note: The enlarged I combines with printed Ba to form IBa, with matoba as the equivalent: the target range or butt. Preserve the capital B and record the I as an initial spanning two physical rows rather than omitting it from the headword.
Ibai, ǒ, ǒta means a horse's neighing. The apparent OCR V belongs to the enlarged I on the preceding row, not this headword; the remaining beginning is Ibai.
Ibara means thorns or thorny growth. The headword begins with capital I in the scan, not the OCR's lowercase i.

runs.text: O ſer arranhado de eſpinhos. Vt,

lines.note: Ibaragaqi is being scratched by thorns. The Portuguese introduces an example with Vt; restore capital I and keep the printed q spelling.
Ibaragaqiuo ſuru illustrates the same thorn-scratching sense. A paragraph sign introduces another example beginning Ibaragaqi, continued on the next row.

Ibaragaqi ni xeraruru describes being scratched by somebody else. The Portuguese compares it with children's behaviour and divides fazem after fa. The very faint terminal point is retained as the baseline stop after reinspection, rather than silently converting it to a hyphen.

runs.text: zem os mininos quando pelejão, & ſe arranhão

lines.note: Zem completes fazem. The example describes children fighting and scratching one another; mininos and the printed nasal marks are retained.

Hũs aos outros no roſto completes the comparison with children scratching one another's faces. The opening is the abbreviated reciprocal expression hũs, not OCR his; the tilde is weak but the surviving letter shapes and phrase support this reading.
Ibari means urine, and Ibariuo ſuru means to urinate. The final Ouri continues into ourinar without a printed hyphen.
Nar completes ourinar. Ibariuo taruru introduces urinating involuntarily, with the lack of awareness specified on the following row.
Sentir completes the description of passing urine without feeling or noticing it. This short row belongs to the Ibariuo taruru example.
Ibaribucuro is the urinary bladder, glossed Bixiga. Restore the visible capital I and preserve the historical Portuguese spelling.

Ibet means another or different thing and ends with the printed label S. At the far right, (mindo. is displaced material completing dormindo from the next physical row; preserve its actual position with separate mark and word spans rather than attaching it semantically to Ibet.

Ibiqi is snoring, and Ibiqiuo caqu means to snore. The gloss Rõcar dor continues as mindo at the far right of the preceding physical row; no text is missing between the entries, and the fragment is not moved into this row.

Ibitçu, with the alternative iybitçu, denotes a box or small container. Restore capital I in place of the OCR's spurious long-s-plus-i; the alternative's printed iy sequence is retained, not normalized.

runs.text: figura ouada em que metem arroz.

lines.note: The container has an oval form and is used to hold rice. This explains the object sense of Ibitçu rather than assuming a general modern sense of irregular shape.
Ibitçu nari is the shape of that box or container. The phrase is a separate printed entry with its own Portuguese gloss, not merely a continuation of the preceding sentence.
Ibo denotes bodily growths or marks, corresponding to warts in the Japanese vocabulary. The source's broader wording Sinais que naſcem no corpo is preserved; the initial is capital I, not OCR ſi.

runs.text: Iboi, ô, ôta, l, vmi, u.

lines.note: Iboi, ô, ôta is paired with vmi, u, suggesting suppuration. The Portuguese describes the working of a cautery point, completed by de fogo below; retain the two circumflexes rather than replacing them with carons by analogy.

runs.text: de fogo. No Ximo ſe diz,

lines.note: De fogo completes botão de fogo. The gloss gives Vbuqe, uru, eta as a regional alternative used in Ximo; Ximo is a Japanese place-name embedded in Portuguese and remains italic as printed.

Ibojiri is an insect called Bicho da ſaude in the Portuguese gloss. The b is damaged but its surviving outline is compatible with Ibojiri; the line does not itself establish a modern species identification.
Ibon is violating a law or order, with tagai and vocaſu as the Japanese equivalents. The headword begins with capital I, and mã- carries an abbreviation tilde before its continuation.
Dado completes mandado, an order or command, followed by &c. and the printed label S. This closes the law-breaking entry.
Iburi describes a bad habit or disposition. The scan reads Ruim cuſtume, not OCR Rouim cuſtame; Ibu- begins the adjectival example continued on the next row.
Rina fito completes Iburina fito, a person of bad disposition. The gloss is about character, not economic circumstances, despite the possible wider senses of condição.
Ibucaxij means doubtful or puzzling. Restore capital I; the following noun and adverb forms belong with this adjective rather than constituting unrelated entries.
Ibucaxiſa is the corresponding noun, doubtfulness or puzzlement. The short indented row supplies no new Portuguese translation and remains associated with Ibucaxij.
Ibucaxǔ gives the adverbial form of the doubtful or puzzling adjective. Preserve the marked long u and the row's separate physical position.
Ibuxei is glossed as something frightening or dreadful. The source's medonha guides interpretation here rather than imposing another modern sense; restore the visible capital I.
Ibuxeſa is the noun, followed by Amarino ibuxeſani meuo fu: the example describes closing one's eyes from great fear. Fu begins fuſaide across the physical line break without an added hyphen.

Saide completes fuſaide, and touotta gives the act of passing through. Feiq. is the printed citation label followed by Lib. 4.; its Portuguese translation begins Com o and continues at the top of column 2.

runs.text: grande medo, paßou com os olhos fechados.

lines.note: The translation begun with Com o at the bottom of column 1 ends here: from great fear, he passed with his eyes closed. Restore the visible continuation indentation and keep paßou with its double-s sort.
Ibuxô is labelled Aduerb., the adverbial form accompanying Ibuxei. The circumflex on o is visible; the source places this row at the ordinary entry margin before the next subsection.

zones.label: Column 2, part 2
zones.note: Enlarged initial I spans the first two body rows.

lines.note: The enlarged I joins printed Ca to form ICa, naming squid or cuttlefish, glossed Chocos, ou ciba. Restore the omitted I and record its two-row span while preserving capital C.
A different Ica is paraphrased by Tçuchibaxino xita, below an earthen stairway. This separate entry begins beside the enlarged I belonging to the previous row, not with a second oversized letter.
The Portuguese completes De baixo da eſcada de terra, below the earthen stairway, and adds the printed label S. Preserve the physical continuation rather than attaching it to the seafood entry.
Icabacari is glossed by Icafodo, asking how much. The Portuguese question mark confirms an interrogative use; the equivalent after i, is not an embedded term in Portuguese.
Icada means a raft. Icadauo cumu illustrates assembling a raft, with Fazer divided after Fa- at the line end.
Zerjangada completes Fazer jangada, building a raft. The source's close setting of zerjangada is retained rather than using the physical line break as an entry boundary.

runs.text: Hũa certa iguaria de peixe crù.

lines.note: Icadanamaſu names a particular dish of raw fish. The line does not supply its preparation, so no modern recipe is inferred; preserve the grave accent in crù.
Icadaxi is paraphrased as Icadauo cudaſu fito, the person taking a raft downstream. The Portuguese starts a description of the person and completes it on the next row.
Completes O que leua, ou guia a jangada: the person who takes or guides the raft. This belongs to the raft-handler entry, not to the next interrogative.
Icadeca asks how or why. Preserve the single printed question mark and the headword's de sequence rather than converting it to a modern spelling.
Icafodo is explicitly labelled as an adverb and glossed Quanto?, how much. A paragraph sign introduces an additional intensive sense, beginning with Mui-.
To completes Muito, with encarecidamente expressing emphasis or insistence. The example permits Icafodo or an alternative completed on the next physical row after l,.
The alternative is icafodomo, not OCR itafodomo; the printed c is recoverable. Mǒxitaredomo means although one said it, and Posto que lho begins the matching concessive translation.

The translation completes the concessive example: although I told him emphatically, nevertheless, and so on. Preserve the source's abbreviated ending &c. rather than supplying an unstated result clause.
Icaga means what or how. Icaga arǒzuru? asks how something will be; the o bears the visible caron and the question continues into the Portuguese translation below.

runs.text: Como, ou de que maneira ſera?

lines.note: The Portuguese asks how, or in what manner, it will be. This is the translation of Icaga arǒzuru?, not a second Japanese example.
Icai describes something large or extraordinary. This adjective is distinct from the following homophonous noun for rank or dignity.
Icai cotouo mita means I saw a great thing. The Portuguese reads Vi, the past-tense verb, not OCR Vt; retain the abbreviation tildes in hũa and grãde.
A separate Icai means rank or dignity, with curai and qizafaxi as Japanese equivalents. Do not conflate this noun with the preceding adjective for great or extraordinary.

Icai tani cotonari is glossed as having higher dignity than others. Retain the printed tani spacing and the terminal digni-; the following physical row supplies only de, an apparent source omission rather than license to add dade.

The scan reads de que os outros. S., completing the comparative gloss. Together the physical rows print digni- / de, not the expected dignidade; preserve that anomalous shortening without inserting an unprinted syllable.

runs.text: Peßoa que come quanto ha como

lines.note: Icamonoguy is a person who eats whatever there is. The explanatory phrase continues with unclean or disgusting things on the next row; keep the historical headword and its final y.
Completes the description of Icamonoguy with unclean things and things that cause disgust. The doubled m in immundas and the spelling aſco are retained.
Icamexij describes something grand and beautiful, or imposing. The Portuguese alternative continues after ou de; the final ij of the Japanese adjective is preserved.
Fauſto completes the imposing or splendid sense. Icamexij fito begins an example of a person making a grand display, with the explanation continued below.

runs.text: faz aparato com os bõs veſtidos, armas, ou ou

lines.note: The display consists of fine clothes, weapons, or other ornament. Preserve the tilde in bõs and the printed ou ou: the second ou begins outro across the next line break without a hyphen.
Tro completes outro, followed by ornato. This closes the example of splendid appearance and is not an independent headword.
Icamexiſa is the noun corresponding to the preceding adjective, grandeur or imposing splendour. It has its own indented row but no separate Portuguese gloss.
Icamexǔ gives the adverbial form of Icamexij. The u carries the visible caron and is not interchangeable with the circumflex o of Ibuxô above.
Icamonozzucuri is a particular construction or style of a great sword. The Portuguese definition continues with de Iapão on the next row; preserve the doubled zz of the headword.
De Iapão completes the specification of a Japanese great sword. Iapão is the Portuguese country name here, not a Japanese term requiring a font-toggle entry.

runs.text: De que maneira, ou como? S. ¶

lines.note: Ican asks in what manner or how and carries the printed label S. A paragraph sign starts Ican to nareba, a causal expression continued on the next row.
To nareba completes the expression, paraphrased by Najenito yǔni. The Portuguese A cauſa starts the explanation that this introduces the reason for something; retain the caron in yǔni.
Dißo he completes A cauſa dißo he, the reason for that is. The double-s sort is retained, and the row remains part of the causal example.

Icana is explained with Icanaru coto or icana coto, asking for what reason. Preserve the printed lowercase i in the alternative and the question mark; these are Japanese equivalents after i, rather than embedded Portuguese terms.

runs.text: que cauſa? &c. Vſaſe eſta palaura estranhã-

lines.note: The gloss asks Por que cauſa? and begins a usage explanation. The word is used when reacting with surprise or objection; preserve the terminal estranhã- and its abbreviation tilde.

runs.text: do algũa couſa, ou negandoa. Poſto que a pro-

lines.note: Completes the usage explanation: reacting to something as strange or denying it. A concessive statement then begins about the fuller or proper expression, divided after pro-.

Pria completes propria. The dictionary identifies Icanaru coto as the fuller expression; this Japanese phrase occurs within the Portuguese explanatory statement and is marked as a whole typeface-toggle term.
Icanaru is glossed Qualquer, any or whichever. Icanaru coto? is then explained as asking what thing or what cause; restore the visible question mark after coto rather than the OCR period.
Completes the interrogative explanation as what thing or what cause, and so on. This row belongs to Icanaru coto?, not to the separate vocative entry below.

runs.text: O: he particula de vocatiuo. ¶ Itẽ,

lines.note: Icani is first treated as a vocative particle, like O used in addressing somebody. A paragraph sign and Itẽ introduce an additional interrogative function.

runs.text: Interrogatiua, Por que? ou de que maneira?

lines.note: The second function is interrogative: why or in what manner. Preserve the capital Por following Interrogatiua and the separate question marks of the two alternatives.

runs.text: Oula oula como quẽ chama a alguẽ

lines.note: Icani icani is a repeated call to somebody, matched by Oula oula in the Portuguese gloss. Restore the faint l in the second oula instead of OCR ou a; retain quẽ and alguẽ with their abbreviation marks and do not add an unprinted final stop.
